Saudi-led coalition claims Houthis targeted power station in Medina
The Saudi-led pro-government coalition in Yemen has claimed that the Houthi rebel group targeted a power centre in Medina in a drone attack on Tuesday, damaging one transformer but leaving the overall electricity network unaffected.
Medina, in Saudi Arabia's western Hejaz region, is among the holiest cities in Islam.
The Houthis, officially called Ansar Allah, have seized territory in Yemen's southwest this month in a rapid offensive triggered by the Saudi bombing of Sanaa airport in July.
The group has also bombed the Saudi East-West oil pipeline, through which Riyadh has diverted oil exports amid Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
But the Houthis previously denied Saudi claims that they had targeted Mecca, the holiest place in Islam.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Who is leading the race for 'the most impossible job on this Earth'?
data.author: Daniel Tester
data.summary:
Who is leading the race for 'the most impossible job on this Earth'?
In April 1953, Norwegian UN Secretary-General Trygve Lie was at New York’s Idlewild Airport to meet his successor. "Welcome, Dag Hammarskjold, to the most impossible job on this Earth," he greeted the Swedish diplomat.
Seven decades later, the UN is about to choose the successor to incumbent Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, for what many regard as one of the trickiest roles on the world stage. Each term lasts five years, usually renewable for a second term.
The next holder of the post is expected to come from Latin America, given how the post rotates between continents (the last Latin American was Peru’s Javier Perez de Cuellar, who left office in 1992). There is also a long-standing, informal push for the UN to appoint a woman for the first time in its 80-year history.
Whoever wins takes on an organisation under strain from multiple directions. Washington, the UN’s biggest contributor, has cut voluntary funding and withdrawn from the World Health Organization (WHO). Elsewhere, worsening financial pressures and unpaid member state contributions have deepened the ongoing liquidity crisis.
Under Guterres, the UN Security Council has been unable to halt or prevent genocides in Gaza and Sudan, or Russia’s war on Ukraine. Furthermore, the US has committed what many regard as breaches of the charter, including abducting and detaining the president of Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro.
The eight candidates each have their own agenda, but common issues have emerged, including the UN being more proactive to prevent potential crises emerging; the need to be a more streamlined organisation; reducing overlapping functions; allowing smaller nations more opportunity to shake off their debt burdens; and the impact of AI and other technologies on the world.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Kushner's financial stakes in Israeli defence firms raises conflict of interest concerns: Report
data.author: Daniel Tester
data.summary:
Kushner's financial stakes in Israeli defence firms raises conflict of interest concerns: Report
US envoy Jared Kushner’s investment firm, Affinity Partners, has the largest stake in an Israeli company invested in more than half a dozen defence companies that have supplied munitions and armaments for the genocide in Gaza and wars on Lebanon, Syria and Iran, according to a report by CNN.
The revelation not only means that Kushner has profited from wars he is officially tapped to negotiate as US President Donald Trump’s envoy, but it means Gulf states including Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar are invested through Kushner’s firm in companies that Israel is using to wage war on Gaza and other Arab states.
Kushner does not have an official position in the US government and is therefore not required to disclose his finances.
Kushner’s link to Israeli defence firms started in 2024 with a $128.5m investment in Phoenix Financial. The company is one of Israel’s largest financial groups, with interests spanning insurance, pensions and asset management. Kushner doubled his stake in Phoenix in January 2025, just five days before Trump was sworn into office. Kushner’s Affinity Partners is Phoenix’s largest shareholder.
CNN found that Phoenix has invested at least $456m in nine companies linked to Israel’s defence sector. Phoenix’s investment in Elbit Systems alone totals at least $265.1m.

Off
Eritrea and Ethiopia have severed all diplomatic ties after accusing one another of engaging in hostile actions, in a major flare-up that could foreshadow another war on the volatile Red Sea.
Ethiopia on Thursday announced it was expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats and closing its embassy in Eritrea’s capital of Asmara, after reports of explosions in Addis Ababa.
The strike punctured Addis Ababa’s relative calm despite Ethiopia’s federal government battling an alliance of rebel movements opposed to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed in Ethiopia’s regions of Tigray, Amhara and Afar.
Western and regional officials in Addis Ababa confirmed to Middle East Eye the sound of explosions in the capital due to a drone strike. AFP reported that the explosion rocked the Ethiopian National Defence Force headquarters in the Tor Hayloch area of Addis Ababa.
In a statement, Ethiopia accused Eritrea of engaging in “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence” against it.
Eritrea said in response it was severing all diplomatic relations with Ethiopia, accusing it of pursuing “an agenda of incessant hostility” against it.
“In parallel with these aggressive intentions, Ethiopia has gone further to host, train, and provide arms to an assortment of what it calls ‘Eritrean armed opposition groups’ to stoke internal conflict for ‘regime change’ in Eritrea,” Eritrea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
Deterioration of ties, risks
Eritrea and Ethiopia have been at odds for months, with regional diplomats warning that ties were deteriorating fast.

US arrests Energy Department employee under claims of backing Yemen’s Houthis
The Justice Department has arrested a man under claims that he attempted to provide material support or resources to Yemen’s Houthis.
The 51 year-old, identified as Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, is a US Energy Department employee.
"As alleged, a US government employee travelled overseas and used his specialised expertise in an attempt to aid the Houthis, a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization backed by Iran," the assistant attorney general for national security, John A Eisenberg, said.
Eisenberg claimed that Ellaboudy "acquired materials for the construction of explosive material and drones capable of delivering these explosives".
"These allegations are so deeply disturbing that they almost defy imagination," he added.
Ellaboudy is scheduled to appear before a federal judge on 2 October in Washington.

data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Trump threatens Iran 'won't be around very long' if no deal reached
US President Donald Trump threatened severe consequences if Iran failed to reach an agreement with Washington, saying that the confrontation with the Tehran will end "very soon".
"Either they’ll do something very proper and smart, or they won’t be around very long," Trump said. "Frankly, I hate to see that, but they won’t be around very long."
Trump also cast doubt on whether Iran can honour the deal.
"When I make a deal with this company, you’re going to honour it. When you make a deal with them, it’s very possible that they won’t honour it," he said.

Senior IRGC adviser says US power in Middle East 'not as portrayed'
A senior adviser to the commander of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said that the US withdrawal from Iraq indicates that Washington's power in the region is waning.
Mohammad Reza Naqdi suggests that the latest move shows that the “power of the United States is not as it is portrayed”.
